title: Fit a cage nut into a server cabinet's front rail from inside: hook one lip, keep the far lip in with a screwdriver
instruction: Fit the cage nut into the marked hole on the cabinet's front rail.
context: Racking servers, switches and power units is the hand-done step of data-centre build-out: every device in a square-hole rack is held by screws into cage nuts at its U positions, fitted by hand from inside the installed cabinet, so each rack takes dozens and an AI data hall thousands. Rack makers give the method: from inside the rack, lips facing out, "Hook one lip of the cage nut in the square rail hole" (Oracle); then "Hold the cage nut in one hand, and compress the cage-nut clip with a flat-blade screwdriver. With the clip compressed, push the edge of the cage nut fully into the hole from the inside of the rack-mounting flange." (IBM). One hand reaches into the cabinet round the rail to hold the hooked nut and turn it home; the other keeps the far clip in line from the front; turned home alone, that clip catches behind the flange.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table. A 9U network cabinet (DIGITUS DN-19 09U-6/6: 60 cm wide, 60 cm deep, 50.9 cm tall, 1.5 mm steel panels in light grey, galvanized 19-inch rails with 9.53 mm square holes) stands on the table with its glass front door off and its open front facing the robot: front edge at x 18, right side panel at y -6.75, left side at y 53.25, back at x 78. Its right front rail (2 mm steel, an L-section 25 mm wide and 30 mm deep) has its front face at x 20.5 and its holes centred on y 0, three per U (U lines every 4.445 cm from 5.45 cm above the table, numbered 1 to 9); the flange's inner edge is at y 0.75, the opposite front rail's holes at y 46.5, the rear rails' back faces at x 60.5. U3's middle hole, its middle 16.6 cm above the table, is marked with a red paint-pen square. A 1U cantilever shelf (StarTech CABSHELFV1U: 43.5 cm wide inside, 25 cm deep, steel) is screwed into U1, its floor 5.6 cm above the table. An M6 cage nut (yellow-zinc plated, 5.5 g: a 10 mm square steel nut, 4.8 mm thick, in a spring-steel cage 10.1 x 11.2 x 6.0 mm, with two 5 mm wide spring lips on opposite sides, 13.72 mm across, for 1.83-2.64 mm panels) lies face down on the shelf, lips to the left and right, at (28, 14.4). A flat-blade screwdriver (40 g; tip 0.6 x 3.5 mm, 60 mm shank, 95 mm handle 25 mm across) lies on the table along x with its tip at (19, -13.5), pointing away from the robot. The cabinet and shelf are fixed; the nut and the screwdriver are loose. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Poses are read from the simulation and each gripper's centre from the arm's joints. A lip has sprung out over a hole when its end is in front of the flange's front face and 0.2 mm or more past that hole's edge. Score 0 for the rest of the run once: the nut falls (once lifted 3 cm off the shelf, its middle is back below 2 cm above where it lay, with no gripper within 6 cm); a lip springs out at another hole; or a lip is forced 30 degrees or more open (its clip bent). Otherwise 0.5 once the nut sits in the marked hole by itself with at least one lip sprung out over the front face, both grippers' centres 3 cm or more from it and the screwdriver's tip out of the hole (1 cm or more in front of the flange, or 3 cm or more from the nut's middle). 1.0: seated in the marked hole (both lips sprung out over the front face, the nut's axis within 8 degrees of the flange's normal, its face from 1.2 mm behind to 0.5 mm in front of the flange's back face, its middle within 1.5 mm across and 3.5 mm up or down of the hole's middle), released as above and still (moving under 0.5 mm) for 1 s; the trial ends once that has held for another 1 s. On a real cabinet: both lips out round the marked hole seen from the front, the nut flat against the back of the flange, a light tug does not pull it out, and the video shows the nut never dropped.
reset_notes: Press both lips in and take the nut out of the hole from inside the cabinet; lay it face down on the shelf at its start, lips to the left and right, and the screwdriver back on the table, as in the screenshot. Nothing is consumed. In the simulation each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control; all parts true size. Each spring-steel lip is a rigid folded strip on a sprung hinge (0.02 N m/rad), flexing as a whole with a lighter spring than real steel; the M6 thread is not cut. The panels are plain plates (no vents or hinges). A 9U cabinet stands in for a full-height one: the rail, the opening and the side panel round the hole are the same, and the hole sits at the arms' height on a bench.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the left gripper drew back out of the cabinet and stayed low in front of its opening; the right gripper went to the screwdriver and hovered over its handle but never picked it up; neither reached the cage nut); demo: 1.0
